title: ms-gateway-api Ocelot timeouts proxying to microservices.methodlocal.int (sync-util / preferences / account paths)

any_of.contains: Unusual number of XHR errors for account

diagnosis: Frontend XHR errors (status_code:0, 'Failed to load') reported to DataDog RUM by method-ui are symptoms â€” the actual failure happens upstream in ms-gateway-api's Ocelot ResponderMiddleware, which raises RequestTimedOutError / TaskCanceledException while waiting for microservices.methodlocal.int (the .NET Framework Tier-3 IIS pool) to respond. Affected paths span multiple owned services on that pool: /syncutil/syncwidget/{account}/GetSyncWidgetInfoAsync, /preferences/v3/User, /account/learning/progress, /account/banners/queue. The pattern is chronic â€” Ocelot warning volume in the 17:00 UTC hour was 1072 today vs 1064 24h ago (+0.7%), so the underlying timeout rate is steady-state, not a regression. DataDog monitor 77419271 ('Unusual number of XHR errors for account: {{@account_name.name}}') trips whenever a single account's user session bunches >40 such XHR errors within 5 min. NOTE: this *may* be downstream of ki-dns-microservices-method-int-pps-quota â€” DNS resolution failures on the Windows fleet manifest as Ocelot timeouts. Cross-reference both before concluding root cause.
playbook: 1) Confirm chronic baseline by comparing ES Ocelot.Responder.Middleware Warning volume in the alert window vs the same window 24h ago â€” if delta < 20%, it's the chronic pattern (no new incident). 2) Aggregate timeouts by RequestPath: if dominant paths are all under upstream microservices.methodlocal.int, it's pool-level. 3) **Check ki-dns-microservices-method-int-pps-quota first** â€” DNS bursts on the Windows fleet present here as Ocelot timeouts. 4) If DNS is clean: identify which downstream microservice owns the slow path via Ocelot config in ms-gateway-api/gateway/API/ocelot.*.json. 5) Decision tree for the fix: (a) raise per-route Ocelot timeout (cheapest, masks symptom â€” appropriate if Ben prefers user-facing reliability over visibility), (b) scale microservices IIS pool / shorten recycle interval (medium cost, addresses cold-start tail), (c) profile the upstream microservice (sync-util / preferences / account) under prod load to find the slow path â€” root-cause fix but expensive.

title: Classic UI app pool crashes from EDA NuGet async-call thread starvation on .NET Framework
diagnosis: Classic UI IIS app pools crash intermittently under high EDA load. Root cause: new EDA NuGet package's asynchronous calls cause thread starvation in older .NET Framework code paths (known limitation in pre-modern .NET). Datadog tracer upgrades and older MassTransit libraries amplify the problem. Load test confirmed: the async version of the NuGet crashes after ~500-600 calls returning 502s; the sync version survives 1000 calls with ~62 timeouts but no crash. Mitigations applied: reduced EDA load and redeployed prior stable code (night of 2026-05-04). A modified sync-only NuGet exists; deployment postponed pending stability.
playbook: 1) Check IIS Event Viewer on PROD-CLASSIC-01/02 for app-pool crashes. 2) Confirm via the absence of explicit error stacks â€” Classic crashes here typically show only pool crashes with no application stack trace. 3) Look at EDA event rate; if elevated, this is the pattern. 4) Mitigation: recycle app pools, or reduce EDA event volume (reduce accounts producing events), or roll back to prior NuGet/Datadog tracer state. 5) Long-term fix is the sync-only NuGet package (built by Matt) â€” deployment pending.

title: DNS resolution failures for *.method.int on Windows fleet â€” AWS Route53 1024 PPS link-local quota exceeded on DCs

any_of.contains: remote name could not be resolved

diagnosis: Every Windows EC2 instance forwards DNS to two AD domain controllers, which then forward *.method.int queries to AWS Route53 Resolver at 172.31.0.2. That destination counts against the AWS per-ENI 1024 PPS link-local quota (shared with 169.254.169.253, IMDS, NTP, Windows Licensing). Combined query rate from 11 Windows hosts pushes DCs' link-local PPS over the cap during bursts; AWS silently drops the excess packets at the VPC fabric. DCs' conditional forwarder for method.int had UseRecursion=True, so on forwarder timeout the DC falls back to root-hint recursion. Root hints can't resolve .int (reserved TLD; no public method.int zone), so they return NXDOMAIN, which the DC negatively caches. Windows DNS clients then cache the negative response for 15 minutes (MaxNegativeTtl), extending visible outage well past the actual packet-drop bursts. ENA linklocal_allowance_exceeded confirms shaping events; CloudWatch NetworkPacketsOut on prod-dc-01 doubled (1,557 â†’ 2,982) at incident time. Affected services: report-generation API, classic API, ms-gateway-api, microservices nodes. NOTE: this can present as ki-2026-05-21-gateway-microservices-timeout (Ocelot timeouts) â€” check DNS first when both fire.
playbook: 1) Check ENA metrics on Windows DCs (prod-dc-01, prod-dc-02): pps_allowance_exceeded, linklocal_allowance_exceeded. If non-zero in the alert window, this is the issue. 2) Check Datadog for NetworkPacketsOut spike on DCs. 3) Confirm the conditional forwarder now points to Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint (rslvr-in-33bec0891b854ea8b at 172.31.223.154 / 172.31.168.212) with UseRecursion=$false â€” the PIR's action items state this was completed on 2026-05-20/21. 4) If the endpoint path was reverted, recycle DNS clients on affected hosts to clear the 15-min negative cache. 5) Long-term per PIR: reduce Windows MaxNegativeTtl from 15 minutes to 30 seconds; enable DNS client logging; collect Datadog throttling metrics (bw_*_allowance_exceeded, pps_allowance_exceeded, conntrack_allowance_exceeded, linklocal_allowance_exceeded).

title: MongoDB rs01 self-aborts on file-descriptor exhaustion (LimitNOFILE=64000 too low)
diagnosis: LimitNOFILE=64000 in mongod.service (never overridden from the install default) is too low for the multi-tenant, one-DB-per-tenant deployment. Migration 716 (commit 23a3164) created two new collections in every tenant DB, pushing FD count past the limit. WiredTiger returned errno 24 (EMFILE), triggering fatal assertion 50882 and a self-abort. The replica set failed over in ~10 seconds, but rs01 stayed down for 91 minutes because Restart=on-failure was not set in the service unit, leaving all traffic on a single data node (causing slow customization screens). rs02 (current primary) was at ~27,300/64,000 FDs and rising at PIR time â€” same crash risk remains until LimitNOFILE is raised.
playbook: 1) Check mongod logs on rs01/rs02/rs03 for fatal assertion 50882 or 'errno 24' or 'EMFILE'. 2) Check current FD usage: `lsof -p $(pgrep mongod) | wc -l`. If approaching 64000, you're on the same path. 3) Check whether LimitNOFILE was raised: `systemctl show mongod | grep LimitNOFILE`. Per PIR action item (Arash, immediate priority), this should be raised to infinity and Restart=on-failure added via systemd drop-in (rs01 first, then step down rs02). 4) Symptom signal: 'customization slow' + only one healthy replica = rs01 (or whichever) is down. 5) Mitigation: manual restart of the failed mongod.

title: QBO Sync silently fails to enqueue to RabbitMQ â€” Datadog trace + old MassTransit blockage
diagnosis: Real-time QBO sync goes silently dark: calls to the QBO Sync API are not landing in RabbitMQ for consumers to process. Recycling the app pool on Sync (Util 2 & 3) is required for messages to enqueue again. Root cause: combination of (a) MassTransit being out of date on the project and (b) Datadog's trace causing a blockage in coordination with MassTransit that prevents messages from going into Rabbit. Mitigation: Datadog's trace has been removed from QBO Sync. A code change by Arash exists to help prevent recurrence when Datadog trace is reattached. MassTransit upgrade is planned as part of the AI Upgrade work.
playbook: 1) If QBO real-time sync is reported as down, check RabbitMQ inbound queue depth for the QBO Sync exchange â€” if the publisher side is silent (no messages landing), this is the pattern. 2) Confirm by checking whether Datadog trace was recently re-enabled on QBO Sync (configuration / deploy history). 3) Mitigation: recycle app pools on Sync Util 2 & 3 (this clears the blockage temporarily). 4) Long-term: keep Datadog trace OFF on QBO Sync until MassTransit is upgraded (tracked under AI Upgrade).

title: Platform slowness from Redis SCAN spikes via CacheClearEventConsumer pattern-deletes
diagnosis: Sporadic platform slowness correlates with Redis CPU/latency spikes. Cause: CacheClearEventConsumer clears cache entries by pattern matching (e.g., 'UserContext:account:identity*', 'PreferenceContext:account:identity*'). On Redis/Valkey, pattern deletes require scanning the full keyspace to locate matching keys. Under high cache invalidation rates (coordinated user/permission changes), this generates burst SCAN commands across multiple shards, saturating Redis and degrading API response times for all customers. Duplicate cache-clear messages for the same account/identity are not coalesced â€” the same expensive scan executes many times in rapid succession.
playbook: 1) Confirm via Datadog Redis metrics: CPU spike + elevated SCAN command rate in the alert window. 2) Check for burst of CacheClearEventConsumer log entries. 3) Mitigation (short-term): no immediate fix â€” slowness resolves when the cache-clear burst subsides. 4) Long-term fix is tracked in PL-62474: (a) replace pattern-scan deletes with tag-based deletes maintaining Redis Set tags; (b) implement message coalescing so burst dupes collapse; (c) add Redis SCAN-rate alerting. Set CachingOptions.RunLegacyCacheClearPatternFallback=true during rollout, flush legacy untagged keys post-deploy, then disable the fallback.
